This vignette takes you from demultiplexed long reads to an AIRR table in
which each consensus receptor sequence has a spatial ID. The next step,
`createSIRUP()`, is in `vignette("SIRUP", package = "SIRUP")`.

The pipeline calls external programs (IgBLAST, pRESTO, vsearch, and MUSCLE).
A vignette cannot run these programs on every computer, so the chunks that
call them show code only. The other chunks run on small samples of the MG
thymus data that come with SIRUP.

## The pipeline

Spatial AIRR-seq libraries are long-read sequencing libraries of receptor
transcripts. Each read carries a spatial barcode, which identifies its spot.
In most protocols it also carries a UMI, which identifies its original
molecule. The processing has two parts:

1. **Demultiplexing**, in the separate [rrad](https://github.com/indianewok/rrad)
   package. rrad finds the barcode and UMI in each read, corrects them against
   the whitelist, and writes them into the read header.
2. **Consensus building**, in SIRUP. `processSpatialSample()` runs these steps:

| Step | Tool | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | IgBLAST (`airrblast::assignGenes()`) | Annotates each read with V(D)J genes |
| 2 | `filterAirr()` | Removes reads that are not receptors or are too short to use |
| 3 | pRESTO `ClusterSets.py` | Groups the reads of each spot by sequence identity (vsearch) |
| 4 | pRESTO `AlignSets.py` | Aligns the reads in each group (MUSCLE) |
| 5 | pRESTO `BuildConsensus.py` | Builds one consensus sequence per group |
| 6 | `airrblast::assignGenes()` and `addGaps()` | Annotates the consensus sequences, adds the IMGT gaps, and writes the AIRR table |

Long-read sequencing has a high error rate. A consensus of several reads
removes most random errors. The spot barcode stays in the sequence header
through every step, so each consensus sequence keeps its spot.

## Install the external tools

You need these programs on your computer or cluster:

* **IgBLAST** (`igblastn`) from NCBI, with its `internal_data` and
  `optional_file` folders.
* **IMGT germline references**, both as IgBLAST databases and as gapped FASTA
  files. The [airrblast](https://github.com/hoehnlab/airrblast) package
  downloads and converts them (see below).
* **pRESTO** (`pip install presto`).
* **vsearch**, which `ClusterSets.py` calls.
* **MUSCLE**, which `AlignSets.py` calls. The SIRUP paper used MUSCLE 3.8.31.

The [Immcantation Docker image](https://immcantation.readthedocs.io) contains
most of them. If you use it, run R inside the container and install airrblast.

Make sure R can find the programs:

```{r check-tools, eval = FALSE}
Sys.which(c(
  "ClusterSets.py", "ParseHeaders.py", "AlignSets.py", "BuildConsensus.py",
  "vsearch"
))
file.exists(file.path("~/share/igblast", "bin", "igblastn"))
```

An empty string means R cannot find that program. Add its folder to `PATH`,
or give its full path to `processSpatialSample()` (`muscle_exec`). SIRUP runs
IgBLAST through airrblast. It always uses `<igblast_base>/bin/igblastn`.

### Build the IgBLAST databases

SIRUP installs the airrblast package. Use it one time to download the IMGT
germlines and build the IgBLAST databases:

```{r build-refs, eval = FALSE}
library(airrblast)
downloadIMGT("~/share/imgt", organism = "human")
imgtToIgblast("~/share/imgt", "~/share/igblast_refs", igblast = "~/share/igblast")
```

`imgtToIgblast()` writes the `database/` and `fasta/` folders into
`~/share/igblast_refs`. Give that folder to `processSpatialSample()` as
`igblast_refs`. If you leave `igblast_refs` out, SIRUP looks for those folders
in `igblast_base`. Give the IMGT folder as `imgt_dir`. airrblast supports
human, mouse, and rhesus monkey.

## Demultiplex with rrad

rrad is a separate package. Install it from GitHub:

```{r install-rrad, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("remotes")
if (!requireNamespace("rrad", quietly = TRUE)) remotes::install_github("indianewok/rrad")
```

`rrad::rad_demux()` finds and corrects the barcodes and UMIs.
`rrad::rad_reformat()` then writes a FASTA file that IgBLAST can read. Choose
the `layout` that matches your library:

```{r rrad, eval = FALSE}
demux <- rrad::rad_demux(
  layout = "five_prime",
  fastq = "reads.fq.gz",
  out_dir = "prepared",
  output = "sample"
)

rrad::rad_reformat(
  demux,
  output_fastq = "prepared/sample-igblast.fasta",
  to_fasta = TRUE,
  header_format = "presto"
)
```

Use `header_format = "presto"`. It puts the barcode and UMI into the read
identifier, which IgBLAST keeps:

```text
>read1|BARCODE=AAACAAGTATCTCCCA|UMI=TCACATTCTGTA
```

`parseRadSequenceIds()` reads these tags into columns. `processSpatialSample()`
calls it for you, but you can use it to check a file:

```{r parse-ids}
library(SIRUP)

headers <- data.frame(sequence_id = c(
  "read1|BARCODE=AAACAAGTATCTCCCA|UMI=TCACATTCTGTA",
  "read2|BARCODE=AAACACCAATAACTGC|UMI=AAAAAGGCTGGT"
))
parseRadSequenceIds(headers)
```

For Visium HD, rrad writes a coordinate barcode such as
`s_002um_00001_00002-1` in place of the 16-base barcode. The
[rrad documentation](https://github.com/indianewok/rrad) explains the Visium
HD layout.

## Look at the read-level data

SIRUP includes 2,000 read-level IgBLAST rows from MG thymus section 2. The
RAD run for these reads wrote the barcode and UMI as the columns
`cell_barcode` and `umi`, not in the header. We enriched this sample for
usable reads: 750 of the rows pass the IGH filter below. In the full
section, only 62,738 of 15.6 million reads (0.4%) pass.

```{r read-raw, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(dplyr)

extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")
reads <- airr::read_rearrangement(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_reads.tsv.gz")
)

dim(reads)
count(reads, locus, sort = TRUE)
```

Most reads are fragments, light chains, or other transcripts. `filterAirr()`
keeps the reads worth building consensus sequences from. These settings
match the SIRUP paper for IGH reads:

```{r filter-reads}
reads$barcode <- reads$cell_barcode

igh_reads <- filterAirr(
  reads,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 100,
  min_j_length = 10,
  min_junction_length = 1,
  productive_only = FALSE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  spatial_id = "barcode"
)

spatialReceptorSummary(igh_reads, spatial_id = "barcode")
```

Keep `productive_only = FALSE` at the read level. A single read can look
unproductive because of a sequencing error that the consensus step corrects.
Filter on productivity after the consensus step. (With `umi_support = TRUE`,
SIRUP builds each molecule consensus from the productive reads of that
molecule.)

`plotLengthQc()` shows the V, J, and junction lengths. Use it to choose the
thresholds:

```{r length-qc, fig.height = 3.5}
plotLengthQc(igh_reads, bin_width = 10, title = "IGH reads, MG thymus section 2")
```

## Run the consensus pipeline

`processSpatialSample()` runs every step from the table above. It prints each
command before it runs it. If a command fails, it stops and shows the command.

You can start from three types of input:

| `input` | `input_type` | First step that runs |
|---|---|---|
| FASTA or FASTQ from rrad | `"auto"` or `"raw_reads"` | IgBLAST on each read |
| AIRR table (path or data frame) from a first IgBLAST pass | `"auto"` or `"airr"` | `filterAirr()` |
| FASTA that is already filtered, with the spot in the header | `"spatial_fasta"` | pRESTO clustering |

### From rrad FASTA

```{r process-fasta, eval = FALSE}
result <- processSpatialSample(
  input = "prepared/sample-igblast.fasta",
  output_dir = "processed/bcr",
  receptor = "ig",
  organism = "human",
  igblast_base = "~/share/igblast",
  igblast_refs = "~/share/igblast_refs",
  imgt_dir = "~/share/imgt",
  muscle_exec = "~/bin/muscle3.8.31_i86linux64",
  identity = 1.0,
  consensus_freq = 0.51,
  consensus_min_count = 2,
  nproc = 8
)

result$db_pass
```

Use `receptor = "tr"` for TCRs. Run BCRs and TCRs as separate calls.

`runIgblast()` calls `airrblast::assignGenes()`, which does not search a
constant-region database. A table made from raw reads has no `c_call` column.

### With UMI support

Reads of one molecule can differ by sequencing errors. At `identity = 1.0`,
those reads fall into different clusters, and each cluster can then fail the
two-read minimum. With `umi_support = TRUE`, SIRUP first groups the reads of
each spot and UMI at a looser identity (`umi_identity`, default 0.95). It
builds one consensus per molecule from the productive reads only. The
spot-level step then combines the molecules and sums their reads.

`umi_support` needs an AIRR table with `umi` and `productive` columns, so give
it the output of the first IgBLAST pass. This is the call we used for the MG
thymus BCRs in the SIRUP paper:

```{r process-umi, eval = FALSE}
result <- processSpatialSample(
  input = igblast_reads,           # read-level AIRR data frame
  input_type = "airr",
  output_dir = "processed/kh02_bcr",
  receptor = "ig",
  identity = 1.0,
  consensus_freq = 0.51,
  cluster_field = "barcode",
  germline_glob = "~/share/germlines/imgt/human/vdj/imgt_human_IG*.fasta",
  igblast_base = "~/share/igblast",
  muscle_exec = "~/bin/muscle3.8.31_i86linux64",
  nproc = 8,
  umi_support = TRUE,
  umi_field = "umi",
  umi_identity = 0.95,
  min_umi_support = 2,
  consensus_copy_fields = "C_CALL",
  consensus_copy_action = "majority",
  filter_args = list(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 100,
    min_j_length = 10,
    productive_only = FALSE,
    complete_vdj = FALSE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL,
    spatial_id = "barcode",
    add_spatial_sequence_id = FALSE
  )
)

result$db_pass_umi
```

With `umi_support = TRUE`, the result has two AIRR tables. `db_pass` holds
every consensus sequence. `db_pass_umi` holds the sequences with at least
`min_umi_support` reads. You can change the threshold later without running
the pipeline again.

### Keep the constant region

The consensus covers the V(D)J region only, so the second IgBLAST pass cannot
call the constant region. To keep the isotype, put the read-level `c_call`
into the FASTA header. Then give `consensus_copy_fields = "C_CALL"` and
`consensus_copy_action = "majority"`. Each consensus sequence gets the
constant region of most of its reads, in `c_call`, and the fraction of reads
that agree, in `c_call_freq`.

### Many samples

`processSpatialSamples()` runs `processSpatialSample()` on each input, with the
same settings:

```{r process-many, eval = FALSE}
processSpatialSamples(
  inputs = c("prepared/slice1.fasta", "prepared/slice2.fasta"),
  output_dirs = c("processed/slice1", "processed/slice2"),
  receptor = "ig",
  igblast_base = "~/share/igblast",
  igblast_refs = "~/share/igblast_refs",
  imgt_dir = "~/share/imgt",
  nproc = 8
)
```

On a cluster, submit one job per sample and chain instead. Each job then
calls `processSpatialSample()` once.

## Choose the parameters

Two parameters have the largest effect on the result:

* `identity` is the similarity that two reads need to go into the same
  cluster in a spot.
* `consensus_freq` is the fraction of reads that must agree at a position. If
  fewer reads agree, the consensus gets an `N` at that position.

A standard Visium spot is 55 µm wide and holds many cells. Two BCRs in the same
spot that differ by one base can come from two related B cells after somatic
hypermutation. For BCRs, use `identity = 1.0`, so that SIRUP does not merge
them. TCRs do not mutate, so a one-base difference in a spot is more likely a
sequencing error. For TCRs, use `identity = 0.99`. In the SIRUP paper,
`consensus_freq = 0.51` gave the most high-quality sequences for both chains.

To compare settings, run `processSpatialSample()` with each value. Clustering
and alignment depend on `identity` only, so with `skip_existing = TRUE` you
can try several `consensus_freq` values and reuse the clustering.

## Filter the consensus table

The pipeline writes the consensus `sequence_id` as `<cluster>,<barcode>`.
The example data include the consensus table of MG thymus section 2. It is
the `db_pass_umi` table that `processSpatialSample()` wrote for the SIRUP
paper:

```{r read-consensus}
consensus <- airr::read_rearrangement(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz")
)
head(consensus$sequence_id)
```

`extractSpatialIds()` copies the part of an ID that a regular expression
matches into a new column. The `suffix` argument adds `-1`, so the barcode
matches the spot names that Space Ranger writes:

```{r extract-ids}
consensus <- extractSpatialIds(
  consensus,
  id = "sequence_id",
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
  suffix = "-1"
)
head(consensus$barcode_10x)
```

`addSequenceQualityMetrics()` adds three columns that help you set thresholds:
`non_N_nucleotide_prop` (the fraction of called bases), `max_gap_length` (the
longest gap in the alignment), and `opening_gap_length`:

```{r quality-metrics}
consensus <- addSequenceQualityMetrics(
  consensus,
  sequence = "sequence",
  alignment = "sequence_alignment"
)
summary(consensus[, c("non_N_nucleotide_prop", "max_gap_length", "consensus_count")])
```

Then filter. These settings match the definition of a quality sequence that
we used to tune the pipeline in the SIRUP paper: a productive rearrangement, a
V alignment of at least 250 nucleotides, a J of at least 30, a junction of at
least 10, and no gap longer than 15 nucleotides.

```{r filter-consensus}
bcrs <- filterAirr(
  consensus,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 250,
  min_j_length = 30,
  min_junction_length = 10,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  max_gap_length = 15,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
)

nrow(consensus)
nrow(bcrs)
```

This table is `db_pass_umi`, so every row already has at least two
reads. In UMI mode, `consensus_count` counts molecules, not reads, so set
`min_consensus_count = NULL` and use `min_umi_support` for the read floor.
Without UMI support, `consensus_count` counts reads. Then use
`min_consensus_count = 2`.

`max_gap_length` depends on the locus. IMGT numbering pads TRBV alignments with
longer gaps than IGHV alignments, so a limit of 15 removes valid TRB
sequences. The SIRUP paper used 15 for IGH and 24 for TRB.

The table is now ready for `createSIRUP()`.

## Visium HD

Visium HD reads carry a 2 µm barcode, such as `s_002um_00001_00002-1`. Most
analyses use 8 µm or 16 µm bins. Space Ranger writes a file that maps each
2 µm barcode to its larger bins (`barcode_mappings.parquet`).
`readSpatialIdMapping()` reads it. Parquet files need the arrow package. You
can also save the file as CSV once and read that.

```{r visium-hd, eval = FALSE}
# bcrs$barcode_2um holds the 2 µm barcode of each consensus sequence.
mapping <- readSpatialIdMapping("outs/barcode_mappings.parquet")
mean(bcrs$barcode_2um %in% mapping$square_002um)

bcrs <- bcrs %>%
  left_join(
    select(mapping, square_002um, square_008um, square_016um),
    by = c("barcode_2um" = "square_002um")
  ) %>%
  rename(barcode_8um = square_008um, barcode_16um = square_016um)
```

Check the match rate before the join. If few 2 µm barcodes match, compare a
few values from each table. The two tables must write the row and column of
the bin in the same order (`s_002um_<row>_<col>-1`).

Load the 8 µm bins with `Seurat::Load10X_Spatial(bin.size = 8)`, and give
`spatial_id = "barcode_8um"` to `createSIRUP()`.

`collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId()` keeps the consensus sequence with the most
reads in each spatial ID and locus. Use it when you expect one cell for each
spatial ID, for example at single-cell resolution.

### Identical sequences in neighboring spots

Transcripts can diffuse a short distance before capture. The same molecule can
then appear in neighboring spots. On Visium HD, where 2 µm bins sit next to
each other, this spatial bleed is common. `collapseIdenticalNeighbors()`
finds groups of neighboring spots that hold the same exact sequence. It keeps
one spot per group: the spot with the highest consensus count, or the spot
nearest the group center if there is a tie.

The function also merges rows with the same sequence in the same spot and
adds their counts. It keeps rows whose spot is not in the Seurat object, such
as bulk rows, without changes.

**Use it on Visium HD data only.** Standard Visium spots are 55 µm wide, 100 µm
apart, and hold several cells each. Two neighboring Visium spots with the same
sequence are more likely two related cells than spatial bleed.

The function estimates the neighbor distance from the spot coordinates. Set
`num_neighbors_non_boundary` to the number of neighbors that a spot in the
middle of the tissue has: 6 on the standard Visium hexagonal grid, 8 on the
Visium HD square grid. The example below runs it on the Visium thymus data
only to show the call and the output:

```{r collapse-neighbors}
thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)

collapsed <- collapseIdenticalNeighbors(
  sirup,
  sequence = "sequence_alignment",
  num_neighbors_non_boundary = 6
)

c(before = nrow(getReceptors(sirup)), after = nrow(getReceptors(collapsed)))
```

For Visium HD, give the 8 µm object and `num_neighbors_non_boundary = 8`.
